title: The letter to Yemen
hook: Maimonides writes to encourage persecuted Jews in Yemen

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rambam's road from Córdoba to Cairo. Your line was from córdoba to cairo. Today, a letter he sent south.

The news from the far south of Arabia is bad. It reaches Egypt in a letter from Jacob, a leader of the Jews of Yemen. A new ruler there is pressing Jews to convert, and some have given in. A preacher who converted is telling people their own scriptures point to his faith. And in one town a man claims to be the messiah, and people are following him. Jacob asks a stranger far away what to tell his frightened community. The man he wrote to had once been a refugee from that very kind of pressure. Today, the letter that came back.
screen: `BAD NEWS FROM YEMEN.` → `PRESSURE, DOUBT, A FALSE MESSIAH.` → `A QUESTION SENT NORTH.`

segments.voice: The answer is known in Hebrew as Iggeret Teiman, the letter to Yemen. The Rambam wrote it in Arabic, the everyday language of his readers, so ordinary people could follow it. And it is warm. He opens with praise for Jacob and the community, and he doesn't scold the ones who are wavering. Then he takes their three troubles in turn. The pressure: hard times have come before, he says, and the people outlasted them; hold on to the covenant and don't lose heart. The doubt: to the claim that their own books point somewhere else, he answers that the verses are being bent out of their meaning, and urges them to keep studying their own texts. The false messiah: gently but firmly, he says this man is not who he says he is, and following him puts the whole community in danger. He judges that the man seems unwell in his mind, and advises the community to deal with him quietly, for its own safety. Near the end, something practical: copy this letter and read it aloud in every community, so no one is left alone with the bad news. Its courage runs back to the Torah. As Moses tells the people in the JPS translation of Deuteronomy: "Be strong and of good courage." Tradition says the Jews of Yemen held this letter dear, and remembered its writer in their prayers. A frightened community wrote to a stranger, and the stranger wrote back as a friend.
screen: `WRITTEN IN ARABIC, FOR EVERYONE.` · `PRESSURE, DOUBT, A FALSE MESSIAH.` · `READ IT ALOUD IN EVERY COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `BE STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Think of one person carrying something hard right now, an illness, a job loss, a lonely stretch, and start a note to them in your head the way the Rambam did: with something true and good about them. Then one plain line of support, and no advice unless they asked. If you pray, you can hold them in your own words first.
Iggeret Teiman. The Rambam's letter to Yemen, written in Arabic so ordinary people could follow it, meant to be read aloud to a frightened community. Today's word.
Your line: write to encourage. A letter can reach people a voice can't. That's day nine hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: The letter to Yemen is studied today as an example of Jewish leadership in hard times, and Yemenite Jews have long honored the Rambam's writings and memory.

Because Arabic was the only language he could write well.

chat.meaning: The Rambam wrote in his readers' everyday language, and asked that the letter be read aloud in every community.
